overview:
Burkina Faso is a landlocked country in the heart of West Africa, roughly the size of Colorado, surrounded by six neighbors: Mali, Niger, Benin, Togo, Ghana, and Ivory Coast. Its name, chosen in 1984, combines words from two local languages and means land of upright, or honest, people. The capital, Ouagadougou, is a sprawling, low-rise city where bicycles and motorbikes outnumber cars and where Africa's largest film festival is held every two years.

About 23 million people live in Burkina Faso, and most of them farm small plots of millet, sorghum, corn, and cotton or raise cattle and goats. French is the official language, but Mooré, Dioula, and Fulfulde are heard far more often in markets and homes. Gold mining has become a major industry. The country has faced serious hardship: since 2015 armed groups have attacked villages in the north and east, forcing more than two million people from their homes, and the military took power in coups in 2022. Despite this, Burkinabè are known for warmth, music, and craftsmanship.
landAndNature: Most of Burkina Faso is a flat, gently rolling plateau of savanna dotted with baobab, shea, and acacia trees. The dry north edges into the Sahel, the semi-desert belt below the Sahara, where the harmattan wind coats everything in fine dust from November to February. The wetter southwest has sandstone cliffs, waterfalls at Banfora, and the strange rock formations of the Sindou Peaks. Three rivers give the country its old name, Upper Volta: the Black, White, and Red Volta, all flowing south into Ghana. Elephants, hippos, and antelope live in the Arly and W national parks in the southeast, and sacred crocodiles in the village pond at Bazoulé are fed by local people who consider them protectors.
peopleAndCulture: The Mossi are the largest people, and their traditional king, the Mogho Naaba, still holds a ceremony in Ouagadougou every Friday morning. Other groups include the Fulani herders, the Bobo, Gurunsi, and Lobi, whose painted mud houses and carved masks are admired worldwide. Most people are Muslim, with large Christian and traditional-religion communities living peacefully together. Tô, a thick millet or sorghum porridge, is eaten with peanut or okra sauce, and riz gras is a festive one-pot rice dish. Music built on the balafon, a wooden xylophone with gourd resonators, and the djembe drum fills celebrations. The FESPACO festival makes Ouagadougou the capital of African cinema, and soccer is the national passion; the team is called the Stallions.
history: Farming peoples settled the region thousands of years ago, and the ruins at Loropéni, stone walls over a thousand years old, show that trading towns once thrived on gold routes across the Sahara. From about the 1400s the Mossi built strong kingdoms with cavalry armies that resisted invaders for centuries. France conquered the area in the 1890s and made it the colony of Upper Volta. Independence came on August 5, 1960. A series of military coups followed. In 1983 a young officer named Thomas Sankara took power, renamed the country Burkina Faso, launched vaccination and tree-planting campaigns, and became a hero to many before he was assassinated in 1987. Blaise Compaoré then ruled for 27 years until protests forced him out in 2014. Since 2015 the country has struggled with violence from armed groups.
funFacts: Ouagadougou is often called the bicycle capital of Africa because so many residents cycle to work and school.
FESPACO, held in Ouagadougou since 1969, is the largest film festival on the African continent.
The ruins of Loropéni, with stone walls up to six meters high, are more than a thousand years old.
Villagers at Bazoulé sit on and feed the sacred crocodiles in their pond, which have never been known to attack them.
A person from Burkina Faso is called Burkinabè, a word that mixes three different languages.
